title: Hong Kong's independent bookstores, a refuge for Chinese readers, are under threat
description: Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.  Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.

Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see the books' covers online after bypassing Beijing's internet censorship using a VPN. At the store, he picked up a title offering a critical account of China. He stood there devouring dozens of pages from another, about a pro-reform Chinese leader who fell from power for sympathizing with the protesters during the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989.

Cheng said he saw perspectives diverging from the mainland's official narrative.

Hong Kong's independent bookstores, many of them tucked away from busy streets inside buildings, have long offered a refuge and a window to a freer world for some mainland Chinese readers seeking ideas suppressed at home.

But these spaces now are under threat following a wave of bookseller arrests over alleged sedition under a 2024 national security law. Critics say their plight reflected the city's broader crackdown on dissent that began after Beijing imposed a separate 2020 security law. Authorities say the two laws are vital to stability.

Greenfield was one of four bookstores targeted by police in just four months. Although bail was granted, the 50-year-old shop in July announced it would close at the end of its lease. Another bookstore, Have A Nice Stay, set up by former journalists, had announced plans to shut down Sunday, citing "elusive red lines" and financial challenges, even before its booksellers were arrested on the same day as Greenfield's.

"If the Hong Kong government desperately tries to bring every aspect of the city into close alignment with the mainland, or even to the point where the two become indistinguishable, that would be a tremendous loss for us mainlanders too," Cheng said.

Hong Kong, a former British colony that returned to China in 1997, was once known for its freedoms of publication and expression.

But in 2015, bookseller Lam Wing-kee and four others affiliated with Causeway Bay Books disappeared. The store was known for selling politically sensitive titles. Lam later told reporters he was held by Chinese authorities, providing explosive details that contradicted official Chinese accounts. Gossipy books about Chinese politics soon dwindled on Hong Kong's shelves.

After the 2020 security law, leading activists were arrested and civil society groups disbanded. Titles about the Tiananmen crackdown and works by pro-democracy politicians were pulled from public libraries. At the city's annual book fair, some smaller book businesses were barred from exhibiting, and a pro-Beijing newspaper labeled an independent book fair a form of "soft resistance."

Despite the pressure and increased official inspections, many pressed on, with some continuing to organize activities alongside selling books.

But the arrests hit Book Punch in March, Hunter Bookstore in June, and Greenfield and Have A Nice Stay in July. The authorities accused the booksellers of selling seditious publications, according to government statements and media reports.

Authorities say statements with "seditious intention" to incite hatred against or the overthrow of the governments of China and Hong Kong are prohibited. But they have not specified the books they consider as "seditious," leaving observers to find clues in news reports quoting anonymous sources.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the law is clear about what constitutes seditious intent and reiterated there would be no banned book list. He said booksellers should ensure the titles they sell do not harm national security, just as those selling food need to ensure the food won't cause a stomach ache or be poisonous.

A bookseller, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of government retribution, said they struggled to judge what was seditious. Still, they became more cautious about whether to sell certain books on China's modern politics. Their landlord was also reviewing whether to continue to rent the space to them after being harassed.

In an emailed reply, the government condemned any "smearing" and false remarks regarding the work in safeguarding national security. It said the security laws clearly stipulate that human rights, freedoms of speech and publication should be protected.

The offenses linked to seditious intention expressly protect expression of opinions or even criticism against government policies, it said.

University student Iris Wang from neighboring Guangdong sensed tighter control over Hong Kong. To her, Hunter encouraged people to think, instead of just selling books like its mainland peers. She bought a postcard about being courageous and a manga there.

Some mainland readers also visit the stores for non-political reasons, such as for their niche books or simply for their calmness.

Hong Konger Brian Leung found companionship in independent bookstores, saying each had its own character. When arrests happened at the shops he visited, he said he felt something he cherished and that Hong Kong deserved was being rejected.

"Part of what I have grown used to in Hong Kong is lost again," he said, adding that the bookshops have not "incited" him because readers can judge for themselves.

In Taiwan, widely seen as the freest publishing hub for Chinese-language books, some publishers have filled the gap as restrictions deepened in Hong Kong after the 2020 security law took effect. Some readers fear one day Taiwan cannot send books to Hong Kong as freely as before.

Taiwan's publishers released six times as many books about Hong Kong between 2020 and 2024 as in the previous five years, according to Cheng Tsu-Bang, a sociology professor at Tunghai University in Taiwan.

"The publication of books seems to have become a very important medium of communication between Taiwan and Hong Kong, or a medium of mutual support," he said.

In July, Taiwan's broadcaster FTV reported that a logistics firm stopped taking orders to ship books from Taiwan to Hong Kong bookstores under investigation. It also demanded a full book list before delivering to other Hong Kong premises, the report added.

One Hong Kong author who moved to Taiwan and has published books there is Lee, who spoke on condition of not using their full name out of fear of government retribution.

Lee has written about Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, saying the independent bookstores served as a bridge to bring works about Hong Kong to the city and connect diaspora writers to their home.

The writer compared the collapse of civil society to a boulder rolling downhill, crushing things in its path. Lee said bookstores were a small flower field where people could breathe and try to safeguard what remained.

"It's now like being told very directly and cruelly that perhaps this borrowed time is coming to an end," Lee said.

title: Star student rejected by 16 colleges, hired by Google, gets legal win in racial discrimination suit
description: A Palo Alto, California, father declares victory after a judge denied the University of Washington's motion to dismiss their anti-Asian bias suit.
fullText:
A father in Palo Alto, California is declaring a victory in court after a federal judge allowed a civil rights lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias in college admissions to move forward.

Nan Zhong and his son, Stanley Zhong, filed federal lawsuits against several elite institutions — including the University of California system, the University of Washington, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University. The complaints allege the universities engaged in "racially discriminatory admissions practices that disadvantage highly qualified Asian-American applicants."

One of their cases will now proceed in part against the University of Washington after a federal judge granted the university defendants' motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part.

"We got an exciting ruling from the judge," Nan Zhong told Fox News Digital. "Effectively, the judge ruled in our favor by denying the university's motion to dismiss. So this is a major development in the lawsuit. That means the judge found enough factual allegations to support our allegation."

Duke Law's Alleged Race-based Admissions Accused Of Defying Supreme Court Ruling: Doj

The ruling centered in part on sovereign immunity. Judge James L. Robart denied the defendants' motion to dismiss Stanley's Title VI claims against the university while dismissing several other claims.

The University of Washington Board of Regents sent Fox News Digital a statement in response to the ruling.

"We're pleased that the court dismissed many of the claims and two of the three plaintiffs. Admission to the Allen School is highly competitive and the vast majority of out-of-state applicants are not admitted because, as Washington's flagship university, we prioritize Washington residents for admission," a spokesperson said.

"With that ruling, we can now proceed into discovery, request internal documents, internal communication, and most importantly, admissions data," Nan said.

Stanley Zhong, now 21, made headlines after he was rejected by 16 of the 18 colleges he applied to — including top-tier public and private institutions — despite boasting an elite academic record. A 2023 graduate of Gunn High School in Palo Alto, Stanley scored a 1590 out of 1600 on the SAT (99th percentile), held a 4.42 weighted GPA, ranked in the top 9% of his graduating class, and had launched a free e-signing startup featured by Amazon Web Services.

Shortly after the college rejections, Google hired Stanley as a full-time software engineer in a position that his family's court filing says typically requires a Ph.D. or equivalent practical experience. Stanley was first scouted by the tech giant in coding competitions when he was just 13 years old.

California Sociology Professor Cited 'Irony' In Removing Act/sat, Not Fixing Racial Disparities As Intended

The family spent over a year researching admissions trends before filing the lawsuits, concluding that anti-Asian bias remains a systemic issue despite recent court precedents.

"The story is much bigger than myself, than my son, Stanley, or our family," Zhong told Fox News Digital. "First of all, I have a younger son, so I don't want him to face the same problem that his older brother faced. I think this is something important we should correct so my future grandkids won't have the same problem again."

Zhong added that since taking their battle public, dozens of families across the country have reached out to share similar experiences.

"After the story came out, we received a lot of communication from other Asian-American families telling us about their story, telling about how highly qualified Asian-American students were rejected left and right," Zhong said. "So this is a large-scale issue and I think of it as an issue that's been around for a long time."

California Board Of Regents To Review Sat/act Testing Ban After 1,400 Professors Warn Of 'Severe' Math Gaps

Spokespersons for the University of California system have previously denied the allegations, maintaining that their admissions policies strictly comply with state and federal laws prohibiting race-conscious decisions.

Stanley Zhong was accepted at the University of Maryland and the University of Texas-Austin but decided to take a job offer as a software development engineer at Google in the fall of 2023 instead.

title: Study conclude social media algorithms negatively influence users mental health
description: | While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health. Dr. Alva Tang, assistant professor of psychology in the School of Behavioral […]
fullText:
While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health.

Dr. Alva Tang, assistant professor of psychology in the School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences, is corresponding author of a proof-of-concept study published online June 25 in Computers in Human Behavior that explores the links between algorithm-recommended content, how that content is processed by the brain and symptoms of depression.

Get the latest news and events delivered to your inbox.

In the study, 60 young adults with an average age of 20 were assessed via validated anxiety and depression scales. They then watched two sets of videos: one of personally recommended videos from their own Instagram or TikTok accounts, which were further categorized for content types; the other of generalized trending videos. Brain activity was recorded using EEG to measure frontal alpha asymmetry — a well-established measure of emotional processing and motivation.

“In frontal alpha asymmetry, dominance on the left represents more positive emotional processing,” Tang said. “Dominant right-sided activity is usually related to more negative processing and withdrawal-related behaviors.

“Instead of after-the-fact reflections, we looked at real-time emotion processing and documented reactions to watching personalized recommendations. In that regard, this study is novel. Prior research on this has been based on survey questions and self-reports. We are reporting what the study participants are looking at and how they are affected by what their feeds serve them.”

The study accounted for total screen time as a confound, or outside factor, which is used in the majority of research on this subject. First author Carole Leung, a doctoral student in cognition and neuroscience, explained that screen time might have weak relations with mental health because that time is not uniformly negative.

“It’s not just about how much time you spend on social media,” Leung said. “What the algorithm recommends to you matters, too. The emotional content in your personalized feed is linked to your brain’s real-time emotional responses and to depressive symptoms.”

Dr. Stacie Warren, associate professor of psychology and a co-author of the study, emphasized the immediacy of the neuroimaging being performed.

“EEG is a real-time processing measure of brain activity within milliseconds,” she said. “Combining brain activity measures with their own reporting on depressive symptoms gives us an objective measure to evaluate what happens as people engage in their algorithmically selected social media.”

The study results confirmed that participants with more depressive symptoms are provided recommendations that lean more depressive, and their brain activity — as determined by frontal alpha asymmetry — is characteristic of depression. This is distinct from their brain activity while watching videos that are trending generally.

“What we’re finding is that if you’re already feeling depressed, then the algorithms reflect that. Continued engagement reinforces this negative feedback loop,” Warren said. “Participants bring in their own phones; we are not selecting videos for them. It’s a new take on understanding how social media consumption affects people.”

The most common category of videos recommended to young adults concerns social relationships, either romantic or friendships. Tang said researchers are finding that the feelings participants displayed could impact the apps’ recommendations.

“If you’re more depressed, you’re more likely to be exposed to a video showing an argument or conflict,” she said. “Positive videos would be about friends supporting each other, for instance. There are videos we classify as neutral as well — those lacking emotional connotation.”

Viewing fewer positive social relationship videos also was associated with relative right frontal alpha asymmetry, or more negative feelings.

“Depressed individuals have a tendency to focus on negative things, dismissing the positive things they encounter,” Warren said. “If you’re depressed and you keep on scrolling, you will encounter fewer positive videos.”

Researchers hope to highlight ways to develop healthy social media engagement behaviors so that negative mood isn’t amplified. The main intervention now is educating people on how to engage with social media more critically and effectively.

“We are teaching teenagers who frequently use TikTok and Instagram how to curate positive content while limiting the negative by following and interacting with the right creators,” Tang said. “If they are tired of their feeds, an account can be set back to default, providing brand-new recommendations. From there, you can reteach the app what interests you.”

Parents also can be more aware of how algorithms influence mood, but limiting teens’ time on social media won’t teach them how to respond in a useful or adaptive way.

“Two years ago, the guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics was to reduce screen time,” Tang said. “These days, if you tell your teenager not to go on their phone, it’s like you’re taking away their life. That’s not going to work.”

Researchers are now collecting data on a cohort of teens ages 13 to 16 for a potential long-term study to understand the emotional effects of algorithm suggestions over time.

Other UT Dallas-affiliated contributors to the current study include Lucie H. Nguyen BS’25, an incoming medical student at Dell Medical School at UT Austin; former UT Dallas research assistant Christina Vlahakos, now a graduate student at Northwestern University; and Dr. Carlos Busso, now at Carnegie Mellon University.

This research was supported by a 2025 Social Sciences Seed Grant from UT Dallas and a Behavioral Health Research Award from the University of North Texas’ Center for Psychosocial Health Disparities Research.

fullText:
In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding

It’s a bleak moment for young people entering the workforce for the first time. For decades, a university degree seemed to promise a stable career – but entry-level white-collar jobs across almost all sectors are being disrupted by AI. Budding accountants, software engineers and junior lawyers increasingly find themselves displaced by cheap automation.

Even creative fields are struggling against AI tech that can produce artwork, lengthy prose or complex design briefs in seconds.

But many young workers have responded by turning to what they see as “AI-proof” heritage crafts. These are the centuries-old, hands-on jobs, such as boat-making, metalwork or bookbinding, that require specialist knowledge built on creative judgment and dexterity, skills not yet mastered by AI.

Eryn Lawley, a 27-year-old politics graduate, said future-proofing her career meant walking away from the digital world. She is now a second-year bookbinder apprentice at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire, learning a trade whose core techniques have not changed for centuries.

“Even just staring at a screen too long was bad for me,” she said. “I always wanted to do something more material, and I think there is something more inherently valuable to something when it is made by a person.”

The work at Ludlow is slow, detailed and tactile. The bookbinding process is almost entirely by hand, using Victorian-built presses, foil-blocking machines and glue brushes.

“People are discovering that, as everything is already decided for you by a computer or algorithm, being able to make or own something physically is good,”

Lawley said. “And it is very satisfying to repeat a task to perfection. It is meditative as a job so it is extremely low-cortisol.”

Paul Kidson, Ludlow chief executive and a fourth-generation bookbinder, said an influx of interest from young people represented a lifeline for a rapidly shrinking industry. He estimates there are now fewer than 50 handcraft-operating bookbinders in Britain today.

“British bookbinding has a terrific reputation across the world, but like so many things in the 50s, 60s and 70s, the training just started to dry up,” Kidson said. “All the formal apprentice schemes collapsed in the early 1980s, and the industry got no training at all.

“We have to train our own people because you can’t recruit at volume because there aren’t any [courses]. Fortunately there is now a desire among a lot of people to want to have the satisfaction of actually making something.”

There is no lack of commercial demand. High-end publishers are betting that shoppers will pay a premium for objects that are crafted by human hands. Joanna Reynolds, chief executive of the Folio Society book publisher – which partnered with Ludlow for a limited edition release of a Game of Thrones book – said the company rejected generative AI tools in its creative processes.

“We do not use AI in terms of our art,” she said. “We believe in the importance of supporting the creative world, and we know there is huge pressure on them at the moment. Their skills and their abilities need to be supported by as many people as possible.”

The number of young people hoping to fill these creative posts is growing rapidly. Cox London, a design house that specialises in artistic metalwork, started its apprenticeship scheme last year. Nicola Cox, a co-founder, said this year the company received more than 160 applications for two apprenticeship places.

“People want to make things and work with materials, [to] have that closeness with it,” she said. “There is AI-proofness about art that is made with someone’s hands. There is a real resonance in something that has a mark and the energy of human hands.”

For Lucky Emerson, an apprentice at Cox London, there is a “worrying feeling” that AI is taking over the creative world.

“The physicality of actually making things is incomparable, especially when people crave originality. Even though technology has advanced, handcrafted art is considered a lot more valuable and will always remain that way.”

Nazifa Tabassum, also an apprentice at Cox London, said she did not think AI would replace her work, but that it could change it.

“For me it isn’t just about making things with my hands,” she said. “It’s about continuously developing my skills, and using technology where it adds value, while still providing the expertise and craftsmanship that people can’t easily automate.

“I see AI as a tool that can assist, but not something that replaces, the satisfaction and value of skilled manual, handcrafted work.”At the National Theatre in London, technical apprenticeships span everything from IT to traditional wig-making, costume design, prop-making and metalwork.

“Our apprenticeships are partly about the need to create a more representative workforce, both for the National Theatre and for the [wider] creative sector,” said Kath Geraghty, head of technical qualifications.

“It is also about plugging the skill gap. These theatre crafts are dying out – our metalworkers are all over 50, wig-making as a skill is really dying. There’s a real need to create our own talent.

“And it’s always been about creating a skilled workforce for the wider creative sector beyond theatre, such as film, TV and broadcast.”

Sarah Ray-Dobson, a 27-year-old apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre, said she felt her practice had been shielded from AI disruption that affected other creative pursuits.

“Everything I’ve been doing for the past two years is very hands-on,” she said. “At my level, it has not been affected by AI.”

But Geraghty adds that, like many employers, the National Theatre is struggling with the huge number of AI-generated applications for its apprenticeship programme.

“We used to think that 100 applicants was a popular apprenticeship,” she said. “In this most recent round of recruitment, we had 728 applications for one role.

“We haven’t yet worked out how to manage it, because it’s not viable for our staff to read 700 applications with care and attention. But the job market that young people are in is difficult, and they are applying for anything they can.”

PARIS, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Nathan Cofnas, the U.S. academic who accused late Cambridge University professor Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been allowed ‌to resume some of his work at Ghent University while a disciplinary ‌probe continues, the Belgian entity said on Friday.

Arday, once hailed as Cambridge's youngest Black professor, was ​found dead at the age of 41 in London this month, days after resigning from his post. Arday had denied the allegation of plagiarism but acknowledged making mistakes.

Ghent University subsequently suspended Cofnas "as a precautionary measure" as it opened an investigation. Cofnas said the ‌probe was into possible discrimination.

In ⁠Friday's statement, Ghent said Cofnas could resume academic activities at the university while the investigation continued on the condition that he worked ⁠remotely and did not engage in any teaching.

The plagiarism allegations against Arday drew huge media coverage, leading to questions about other elements of Arday's life, including statements he made ​about his ​career, personal life and medical conditions.

GHENT SAYS ​IT HAD CONTACT WITH U.S. AMBASSADOR

Ghent ‌also said it had been in contact with the U.S. ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, about Cofnas.

"Ghent University confirms that it has been in contact with the U.S. Ambassador," it said via email, confirming a social media post by White.

Cofnas wrote in a post on X late on Thursday that his suspension period was over, ‌thanking White for taking an interest in his ​case.

Cofnas arrived at Ghent after Cambridge University's Emmanuel ​College ended its association with him ​after some students expressed concerns over Cofnas' blog posts, which argued ‌that in a meritocracy "blacks would disappear ​from almost all high-profile ​positions outside of sports and entertainment".

Cofnas says he is not a racist and is in legal dispute with Emmanuel College.

Arday's death triggered intense debate about ​racism in the academic ‌world and the media in Britain.

Before his death, Arday repeatedly said the ​public attacks upon him were taking a toll on him and his ​family.

title: Florida Students Punished for Silent Protest Against ICE Get Free Speech Victory in Federal Court
description: A federal judge sided with the Florida International University students who sued over their school's student expression policy.
fullText:
A group of Florida students returning to college may have scored a temporary free speech win, but their legal battle may not be over.

On Sunday, a federal judge ruled that Florida International University (FIU) likely violated students' free speech rights when the school punished students for silently protesting indoors, reported Axios. In her ruling, U.S. Southern District of Florida Judge Jacqueline Becerra issued a preliminary injunction, preventing the school from enforcing its expressive activity rule against the students.

The case stems from an incident in March when a group of students wearing shirts saying "ICE OFF FIU" stood in silence for "a few minutes" while the school's president hosted a talk with former MLB player Alex Rodriguez on campus, reported WLRN. The students were protesting the "school's voluntary collaboration with immigration enforcement on campus," the outlet reported. 

FIU charged seven of the students who participated with misconduct, and six received written reprimands. The school also ordered the students to record two-minute "video reflections" explaining their understanding of the school's expressive activities policy and how they will "apply" what they "learned moving forward."

The disciplinary action drew the attention of civil liberties organizations, including the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). On June 18, the group sent a letter to FIU urging the school "to drop the conduct charges and revise its expressive activities policy to protect such expression inside university facilities."

The school did not take action. On August 11, the punished students sued the school and members of its administration. In addition to requesting compensatory damages, the suit argued that FIU's Regulation 110(3)—which prohibits "protests, parades, marches, picketing, demonstrations, and other similar expressive activities" inside university buildings—"blatantly violate[d] the Plaintiffs' First Amendment rights" and should be declared unconstitutional. The rule also states that "university indoor facilities are designed for instruction, study, reflection, group discussion, research, administrative functions, and other University activities and operations," and "this provision will be enforced in a content and viewpoint neutral manner."

Becerra, citing the Vietnam War-era free speech case Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, found that the plaintiffs were "substantially likely to prevail" in their challenge against FIU's unconstitutional policy. The ruling also notes that "based on the evidence submitted to date, it does not appear that any Plaintiff, or anyone else wearing an 'ICE OFF FIU' T-shirt, spoke or did anything other than sit, stand, and walk."

According to Inside Higher Ed, university officials have "previously maintained that the policy is compliant with the First Amendment and Florida laws." It's unclear whether FIU will appeal. A school representative told Axios that the university would "comply with the court's order while considering our legal options." 

Regardless of whether one agrees with the students' message, FIU's punishment of the silent protesters should concern free speech defenders. Perhaps the most disturbing part of FIU's punishment was forcing students to record video apologies for silently and non-disruptively expressing their views. Bret Weinstein, a longtime opponent of campus cancel culture, weighed in on the situation, writing on X, "Commitment to freedom of speech requires us to oppose compelled speech every bit as strongly as we oppose censorship." Hopefully, by this school year, other universities will adopt this principled stance.

The post Florida Students Punished for Silent Protest Against ICE Get Free Speech Victory in Federal Court appeared first on Reason.com.

fullText:
Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided

Neurosurgeons in London have performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.

The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.

While the surgical team remained in full control, the AI system analysed live camera footage during the operation, helping identify key structures such as nerves and blood vessels that should be avoided near the 11mm (0.4in) tumour on Hibbert’s pituitary gland.

“When I came round … I could see everything in the room clearly,” said Hibbert, who was able to walk independently without glasses or sticks within a week of the surgery.

He has since returned to work as a customer service manager. “It feels like I’ve got a 360‑degree panoramic view of everything around me,” he said.

The surgeons operated on Hibbert using new AI technology which helps to identify tiny anatomy in the brain by colour-coding important structures to help surgeons recognise them safely.

The hospital had previously used the technology as a research tool but the operation was the first time it had been used on a patient.

The pituitary gland, blood vessels and nerves controlling vision are tightly packed together, and “going a millimetre wrong can make a critical difference”, health officials said, potentially leading to blindness, stroke or death.

Dr Sophia Bano, an associate professor in robotics and AI at UCL and the technical lead for the AI system, said: “By learning from hundreds of surgical videos, [the system] has been exposed to a breadth of surgical examples that would take a surgeon many years to encounter.

“It is designed to help recognise critical anatomy, surgical instruments and tissue interactions in real time, supporting the surgeon during highly delicate procedures.”

Initially managed without surgery, Hibbert’s symptoms had worsened since his diagnosis in 2024, and included severe hormone imbalance and vision problems. Without the operation, he faced going blind, health officials said.

Hibbert, from Bedfordshire, said: “The NHNN was founded in 1859 … and was the world’s first dedicated neurosurgical hospital. So to me, it seems very fitting that the same hospital should also be the world’s first to carry out an AI-assisted neurosurgery.”

Prof Mike Lewis, the scientific director for innovation at the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), which funded the operation as part of a clinical trial, said the “pioneering surgery” highlighted the potential of advanced AI to support surgeons and improve patient care.
